transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I guess what finally got me to come in is that this thing with wasps has gotten bigger than I can manage. I don’t mean I just don’t like them — nobody likes getting stung — but I’ve gotten to where I’m planning my whole summer around avoiding them. 

I used to help with garden jobs at church, you know, pulling weeds, tidying up outside, that sort of thing, and I’ve basically given that up because I’m afraid there’ll be wasps around. And at home, if I hear buzzing near the back porch, I won’t even go out there. I’ll have my husband unload things instead, even if it’s inconvenient or silly-looking. It’s embarrassing, honestly, but it’s running more of my life than I want it to.
Do you ever have panic or anxiety attacks when you encounter wasps or think you might encounter them?

Yes… I don’t know if I’d call them attacks exactly, but it comes on so fast. The second I hear that sharp buzzing by the porch, or if I see one hovering around the flowers, my heart just sort of jumps into my throat. My hands start shaking, and all I can think is, “Get inside, get away from it.”

It’s not like I have time to reason with myself. I can be perfectly fine one minute, carrying something or looking out the window, and then that buzzing sound happens and my whole body reacts before I even think. I’ll drop what I’m doing or back away, and I feel like I have to get indoors right away. It feels immediate, like my body is sounding an alarm.
Are you afraid of other insects besides wasps?

Not really, no… I mean, I don’t love bugs in general, but it’s not the same thing. A spider in the corner or a beetle on the sidewalk might make me wrinkle my nose, but I can usually deal with that.

With wasps, it’s different. I know, logically, it’s just a little insect, and I know most people would just swat it away or step back and not make a whole production of it. But for me, if one gets near me, it feels like something awful is about to happen. Like my mind jumps straight to danger, even if I’m telling myself, “It’s tiny, it’s outside, it’s probably not even interested in you.” It doesn’t matter in the moment. It feels terrible, like I have to get away before something bad happens.
Are there any other situations or activities that you avoid because of fear or anxiety, besides those related to wasps?

No, not really outside of the wasp thing. I mean, I’m here because it’s gotten to where my whole summer feels like it revolves around avoiding them. I’ve stopped doing the garden work at church, which I used to help with, because I just can’t stand the thought of being out there and having one come near me.

And even at home, if I hear buzzing by the back porch, I won’t go out. I’ll ask my husband to unload things or handle whatever needs doing out there, even if it’s something I should be able to do myself. So it’s not that I’m avoiding all kinds of places or activities generally — it’s really the situations where I think wasps might be around.
Are you afraid of being stung by wasps or is it something else about them that frightens you?

I suppose the sting is part of it, yes, because nobody wants to be stung, but it feels bigger than just that. I know a wasp is just a little insect, and most folks would probably swat it away or step back and not think much more about it. But when one gets anywhere near me, it feels like something terrible is about to happen.

It’s hard to explain because I can hear how silly it sounds when I say it out loud. It’s not like I’m sitting there calmly thinking, “Oh, that might sting me.” It’s more like my whole mind jumps straight to danger, like this awful thing is right there and I have to get away from it immediately.
Do you ever have recurring thoughts about wasps that you can't seem to get out of your head?

I don’t think so… not in the way you mean, I don’t think. I mean, I’ll think about them if I know I’m going somewhere they might be, like if someone says we’re eating outside or I see the weather getting warm and people are putting food out. Then I might start thinking, “Oh Lord, what if there are wasps around?” But it’s more tied to the situation, if that makes sense.

I don’t just sit at home in the evening and have wasp thoughts coming into my head over and over for no reason. It’s not like I’m trying to push an image out of my mind all day. It’s more that if something reminds me of them, or I hear buzzing, or I’m about to go outside, then my mind goes there pretty quickly. But recurring thoughts out of nowhere… no, I don’t think I’ve noticed that.
Have you ever had a similar intense fear reaction to any other animal, not just insects?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’m not especially fond of snakes or mice or things like that, but I think a lot of people aren’t, you know? If I saw a mouse in the house I’d probably holler and want my husband to deal with it, but it’s not that same feeling.

With wasps it’s different. It’s like my body reacts before I even have time to think. With other animals, I might be startled or uncomfortable, but I don’t usually feel that same urgent need to get away right that second. So no, I can’t really think of another animal that does that to me the way wasps do.
Is your fear more of the wasp itself or of being stung by it?

It’s both, I suppose, but if I’m being honest, it feels more like the wasp itself. The sting is part of what I’m afraid of, of course, but it’s not just a sensible thought like, “Oh, that might hurt.” It’s the moment I see one near me, my whole body seems to read the wasp as danger.

I know, logically, it’s just a little insect. Most people would maybe wave it away or move their drink and carry on. But for me, if one gets anywhere near me, it feels like something terrible is about to happen right then, like I need to get away from it before I can even think properly.
Is your fear of wasps triggered by seeing pictures or videos of them, or is it only when you encounter them in real life?

It’s much more when it’s real, when one is actually near me. A picture or a video might make me uncomfortable, like I’ll look away or feel a bit bothered, but it doesn’t hit me the same way.

The real thing is different because it’s the movement and the sound, I think. The second I hear that sharp buzzing by the porch, or I see one hovering near the flowers, my heart just jumps. My hands start shaking, and I feel like I have to get inside right away. It’s not even a long thought process. I don’t sit there thinking, “Is that a wasp, could it sting me?” It’s just—there it is, and my body says get away now.

So no, pictures aren’t really the main problem. It’s when I encounter them in real life, especially if they’re close to me or flying around where I’m standing.
Is it the way the wasp looks or its movement and buzzing sound that triggers your fear?

It’s more the movement and the buzzing, definitely. I mean, I don’t like the way they look either, that skinny body and the yellow and black, but the real trigger is when it’s moving around me.

The second I hear that sharp buzzing by the porch, or I see one hovering near the flowers, it’s like my body reacts before I can even sort out what I’m seeing. My heart jumps, my hands start shaking, and I just feel this strong need to get inside right away. It’s not really me calmly thinking, “That’s a wasp.” It’s more like the sound or the way it darts around sets me off immediately.
Is it the possibility of being stung that scares you most when you encounter a wasp?

Not exactly, no. I mean, I do think about being stung, and I don’t want that to happen, obviously. But it’s not only that specific thought that scares me most.

It’s more that when I see a wasp near me, I just feel like something awful is about to happen. I know it sounds out of proportion, because it’s just a little insect and other people would probably swat it away or step aside and not make a big deal of it. But for me, if it comes anywhere near me, my mind and body react like I’m in real danger right then. The sting is part of it, but the fear feels bigger than just “that might hurt.”
Is your fear of wasps limited to a specific type, such as yellowjackets or hornets, or is it any wasp in general?

It’s not really one kind, no. I don’t think I’m calm with some and only afraid of yellowjackets or hornets or anything like that. If I recognize it as a wasp—or even if I’m pretty sure it’s one—that’s enough.

I know, logically, a wasp is just a little insect, and most people would probably just swat it away or move aside and not think much more about it. But for me, if one gets anywhere near me, it feels like something terrible is about to happen. So it’s more any wasp in general, not a specific type.
Has your fear of wasps affected your relationships with family or friends?

Yes, it has, more than I like to admit. I wouldn’t say people have stopped talking to me or anything dramatic like that, but it has changed how I spend time with them.

I used to be part of the church gardening group, and that was one of my main ways of seeing people and feeling useful, you know? We’d be out there planting, weeding, talking while we worked, and I really enjoyed that. But because of the wasps, I’ve had to step back from it. I just couldn’t handle being out there when they were around the flowers or the beds, and after a while it became easier to stop going than to keep making excuses or getting upset.

And I also stopped hosting little garden days at my house. I used to have people over, family or friends, and we’d work in the yard or sit outside afterward. That was a big part of how I stayed connected with people. Now I avoid planning things like that, because I’m worried a wasp will show up and I’ll react badly or have to run inside.

At home, my husband has taken over a lot of the porch and garden things I used to do myself. I’m grateful, of course, but I don’t like feeling like I’ve handed over parts of my own home life because I can’t manage them anymore. So yes, it has affected relationships, mostly by making me pull back from people and depend on my husband more.
Have you avoided any other activities or situations besides gardening and spending time on your porch due to your fear of wasps?

Yes. It’s gotten bigger than just the garden or the porch, honestly. I plan a lot of my summer around whether I think wasps might be around, which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud, but that’s what I do.

If there’s something that needs to be done outside or near the back porch, I’ll try to time it for when I think they won’t be active, or I’ll avoid it altogether. And if I hear buzzing near the back porch, I just freeze up or go back inside. There have been times when we’ve brought things home—groceries, supplies, whatever—and if I hear that buzzing sound or think I saw one, I’ll make my husband unload things instead of me doing it. I feel bad about that, because it’s not like I’m incapable of carrying bags, but in that moment I just can’t make myself stay there.

So yes, it’s not only gardening. I’m here because it’s gotten to where I’m arranging my whole summer around avoiding them, and that’s not how I want to be living.
Does your fear of wasps affect your daily routine during other times of the year, not just during summer?

I’m not sure, honestly. I notice it much more in the warmer months, because that’s when I expect them to be around and I’m outside more. During the colder parts of the year, I don’t think my routine changes in the same way.

I mean, I’m probably still aware of it in the back of my mind if I’m thinking ahead to spring or summer, but day to day in winter or when it’s cold, I can’t say it affects me the same way. It’s really when there’s a realistic chance I might run into one that I start planning around it.
Do you ever worry about wasps during the winter months when you're not seeing them?

Not really, no—not in the same way. In winter, if I’m not seeing them and I’m not hearing them, I don’t usually sit around worrying that one is going to appear.

I might have a passing thought now and then, like if the weather starts changing or I’m thinking about what needs doing outside when spring comes, but it’s not something that takes over my day in the winter. It’s more like… I know the problem is still there, but it’s quiet because I’m not being faced with them. So I wouldn’t say I’m actively worrying about wasps in the winter months, at least not much.
Has your fear of wasps caused you any problems at work or affected your ability to participate in hobbies or other activities you enjoy?

Yes, it has. I’m not working, so it’s not really a job issue for me, but it has affected the things I used to do and enjoy.

The biggest one is the church gardening group. I used to be pretty involved with that. It wasn’t just about flowers or pulling weeds, you know—it was a way I stayed connected with people. We’d talk while we worked, share plants, sometimes make a whole morning of it. But I’ve had to step back from that because I just can’t relax out there anymore if I’m worried about wasps being around. I feel embarrassed even saying that, because it sounds like such a small thing, but it changed something that was important to me.

And I used to host little garden days at my house too, where people would come over and we’d work in the garden or sit out after. I stopped doing that. I make excuses or just don’t plan them anymore, because the thought of being responsible for people being outside near my porch or garden, and then a wasp showing up, it’s just too much.

At home, my husband has taken over a lot of the porch and garden tasks I used to do myself. Things I didn’t think twice about before, I now avoid or ask him to handle. So it’s definitely affected my routines and the parts of my life that helped me feel useful and connected.
Has your fear of wasps significantly impacted your overall quality of life?

Yes, I would say it has, more than I like to admit. It’s not like every single part of my life is ruined or anything, but it has taken away things that mattered to me.

The church gardening group was a big one. I used to really enjoy that—not just the gardening itself, but being with people, feeling like I was helping, having that regular connection. And I’ve stepped back from it because I just don’t feel comfortable out there anymore. I’m too distracted by the possibility of wasps being around.

And then at home, I stopped hosting those little garden days I used to do. That used to be such a nice thing for me, having people over and spending time outside together. Now I just don’t plan them. My husband has also taken over porch and garden jobs I used to do myself, which makes me feel a bit helpless sometimes.

So yes, I think it has affected my quality of life. Maybe not in a dramatic way from the outside, but for me it’s changed my routines and made my world feel smaller.

I’m grateful, of course, but I don’t like feeling like I’ve handed over parts of my own home life because I can’t manage them anymore. So yes, it has affected relationships, mostly by making me pull back from people and depend on my husband more.

doctor.intent: Determine the level of avoidance in daily life due to the fear of wasps
doctor.question: Have you avoided any other activities or situations besides gardening and spending time on your porch due to your fear of wasps?

target_item.name: Phobic_Avoidance_Endure
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because I’ve gotten to where I plan my whole summer around avoiding wasps, even giving up my garden jobs at church and making my husband unload things by the back porch if I hear buzzing.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the fear leads to avoidance of additional activities or situations, which directly concerns active avoidance due to the phobic object.

patient.answer:
Yes. It’s gotten bigger than just the garden or the porch, honestly. I plan a lot of my summer around whether I think wasps might be around, which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud, but that’s what I do.

If there’s something that needs to be done outside or near the back porch, I’ll try to time it for when I think they won’t be active, or I’ll avoid it altogether. And if I hear buzzing near the back porch, I just freeze up or go back inside. There have been times when we’ve brought things home—groceries, supplies, whatever—and if I hear that buzzing sound or think I saw one, I’ll make my husband unload things instead of me doing it. I feel bad about that, because it’s not like I’m incapable of carrying bags, but in that moment I just can’t make myself stay there.

So yes, it’s not only gardening. I’m here because it’s gotten to where I’m arranging my whole summer around avoiding them, and that’s not how I want to be living.

doctor.intent: determine if the fear of wasps interferes with the patient's daily routine beyond summer activities
doctor.question: Does your fear of wasps affect your daily routine during other times of the year, not just during summer?

target_item.reason: The question asks whether the fear affects daily routine during other times of the year outside summer, but the symptom profile only describes avoidance and routine changes during summer/wasp-active situations and does not specify impact in other seasons.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure, honestly. I notice it much more in the warmer months, because that’s when I expect them to be around and I’m outside more. During the colder parts of the year, I don’t think my routine changes in the same way.

I mean, I’m probably still aware of it in the back of my mind if I’m thinking ahead to spring or summer, but day to day in winter or when it’s cold, I can’t say it affects me the same way. It’s really when there’s a realistic chance I might run into one that I start planning around it.

doctor.intent: determine if fear is persistent across seasons
doctor.question: Do you ever worry about wasps during the winter months when you're not seeing them?

target_item.reason: The question asks about whether I worry about wasps during winter when they are not present, but the provided symptom profile does not include a specific item about off-season or anticipatory worry in the absence of exposure.

patient.answer:
Not really, no—not in the same way. In winter, if I’m not seeing them and I’m not hearing them, I don’t usually sit around worrying that one is going to appear.

I might have a passing thought now and then, like if the weather starts changing or I’m thinking about what needs doing outside when spring comes, but it’s not something that takes over my day in the winter. It’s more like… I know the problem is still there, but it’s quiet because I’m not being faced with them. So I wouldn’t say I’m actively worrying about wasps in the winter months, at least not much.

doctor.intent: determine if the fear is causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational areas of life beyond what's already been described
doctor.question: Has your fear of wasps caused you any problems at work or affected your ability to participate in hobbies or other activities you enjoy?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve had to step back from the church gardening group and stopped hosting garden days, which used to be a big part of how I stayed connected with people. At home, my husband has taken over porch and garden tasks I used to handle myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the wasp fear has caused problems with work, hobbies, or enjoyable activities, which directly concerns functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes, it has. I’m not working, so it’s not really a job issue for me, but it has affected the things I used to do and enjoy.

The biggest one is the church gardening group. I used to be pretty involved with that. It wasn’t just about flowers or pulling weeds, you know—it was a way I stayed connected with people. We’d talk while we worked, share plants, sometimes make a whole morning of it. But I’ve had to step back from that because I just can’t relax out there anymore if I’m worried about wasps being around. I feel embarrassed even saying that, because it sounds like such a small thing, but it changed something that was important to me.

And I used to host little garden days at my house too, where people would come over and we’d work in the garden or sit out after. I stopped doing that. I make excuses or just don’t plan them anymore, because the thought of being responsible for people being outside near my porch or garden, and then a wasp showing up, it’s just too much.

At home, my husband has taken over a lot of the porch and garden tasks I used to do myself. Things I didn’t think twice about before, I now avoid or ask him to handle. So it’s definitely affected my routines and the parts of my life that helped me feel useful and connected.

doctor.intent: Determine if the fear of wasps is causing significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life
doctor.question: Has your fear of wasps significantly impacted your overall quality of life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve had to step back from the church gardening group and stopped hosting garden days, which used to be a big part of how I stayed connected with people. At home, my husband has taken over porch and garden tasks I used to handle myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the fear has significantly affected overall quality of life, which is most directly about functional impairment in activities, social connection, and home responsibilities.

patient.answer:
Yes, I would say it has, more than I like to admit. It’s not like every single part of my life is ruined or anything, but it has taken away things that mattered to me.

The church gardening group was a big one. I used to really enjoy that—not just the gardening itself, but being with people, feeling like I was helping, having that regular connection. And I’ve stepped back from it because I just don’t feel comfortable out there anymore. I’m too distracted by the possibility of wasps being around.

And then at home, I stopped hosting those little garden days I used to do. That used to be such a nice thing for me, having people over and spending time outside together. Now I just don’t plan them. My husband has also taken over porch and garden jobs I used to do myself, which makes me feel a bit helpless sometimes.

So yes, I think it has affected my quality of life. Maybe not in a dramatic way from the outside, but for me it’s changed my routines and made my world feel smaller.
